q: What resistance level (as % of maximal lifting ability) is optimal for a strength-training program?
explanation:
For optimal strength-training results, resistance should be 60% to 80% of maximal lifting ability (p824).

B. 40% to 50%: This is the lower starting resistance for older adults learning the movements (p824); the requested value is 60% to 80% (p824).
C. 7% to 10%: This is neuropathic pain prevalence, not a resistance-training prescription (p1056); the requested value is 60% to 80% (p824).
D. 15% to 30%: This is the reported improvement in peak oxygen consumption with cardiac rehabilitation (p830); the requested value is 60% to 80% (p824).

q: How much knee flexion is required to climb stairs with a normal reciprocal gait?
o: At least 120 degrees
At least 90 degrees
At least 150 degrees
No knee flexion is required
explanation:
Climbing stairs with a reciprocal gait requires at least 90 degrees of knee flexion (p825).

A. At least 120 degrees: 120 degrees is the lower end of shoulder flexion/abduction for overhead reaching, not the knee requirement (p825); the requested value is at least 90 degrees (p825).
C. At least 150 degrees: 150 degrees is the upper end of the shoulder range for overhead reaching, not the knee requirement (p825); the requested value is at least 90 degrees (p825).
D. No knee flexion is required: The stair task explicitly requires knee flexion (p825); the requested value is at least 90 degrees (p825).

q: What is the mnemonic for using a cane on stairs after a unilateral lower-extremity injury?
o: Up with the bad and down with the bad
Up with the good and down with the bad
Up with the good and down with the good
Up with the bad and down with the good
explanation:
Patients using a cane on stairs are taught to go up with the good limb and down with the bad limb (p827).

D. Up with the bad and down with the good: This reverses both instructed lead limbs (p827).
C. Up with the good and down with the good: Descent starts with the involved limb and cane, not the uninvolved limb (p827).
A. Up with the bad and down with the bad: Ascent starts with the uninvolved limb, not the involved limb (p827).

q: What fraction of eligible patients receive cardiac rehabilitation?
o: Approximately 20%
Approximately one-third
Approximately 16%
Approximately 25%
explanation:
Approximately one-third of eligible patients receive cardiac rehabilitation despite its benefits (p830).

C. Approximately 16%: This is the five-year mortality of CR participants in the Medicare cohort (p830); the requested value is approximately one-third (p830).
D. Approximately 25%: This is the five-year mortality of nonparticipants in that cohort (p830); the requested value is approximately one-third (p830).
A. Approximately 20%: This is the reduction in five-year mortality with at least 25 sessions (p830); the requested value is approximately one-third (p830).

q: How long must a heart failure patient be clinically stable before starting cardiac rehab?
o: At least 3 to 4 weeks
24 to 48 hours
At least 6 months
2 months
explanation:
Before exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation, heart-failure patients must be clinically stable with controlled fluid status for at least 3 to 4 weeks (p830).

B. 24 to 48 hours: This is the earliest interval for poststroke rehabilitation once medically stable (p831); the requested value is at least 3 to 4 weeks (p830).
C. At least 6 months: This is the exercise-program duration for peripheral arterial disease benefit (p830); the requested value is at least 3 to 4 weeks (p830).
D. 2 months: This is how early quality-of-life improvement may be seen after starting CR (p830); the requested value is at least 3 to 4 weeks (p830).

q: When can stroke rehabilitation safely begin after a stroke?
o: After a required minimum delay of 3 to 4 weeks once medically stable
After a required minimum delay of 6 months once medically stable
As early as 24 to 48 hours poststroke once the patient is medically stable
Before the patient is medically stable
explanation: Stroke rehabilitation may begin as early as 24 to 48 hours once medically stable (p831). A required delay of weeks or months is not the stated timing; starting before medical stability also fails the condition. Only the unchanged key gives the book timing and condition.

q: What proportion of stroke patients develop hemiplegic shoulder pain?
explanation:
Hemiplegic shoulder pain affects 34% to 84% of patients after stroke (p831).

A. 50% to 70%: This is first-month bladder incontinence after stroke (p831); the requested value is 34% to 84% (p831).
D. 15% to 70%: This is the reported incidence of poststroke depression (p831); the requested value is 34% to 84% (p831).
B. 60% to 80%: This is phantom limb pain after lower-extremity amputation (p830); the requested value is 34% to 84% (p831).

q: What hip-flexion angle should be avoided after posterolateral-approach total hip arthroplasty during early recovery?
o: More than 90 degrees
No limitation on hip flexion
Only less than 90 degrees
Only 120 to 150 degrees
explanation:
During early recovery after posterolateral hip arthroplasty, patients may need to avoid hip flexion beyond 90 degrees to reduce dislocation risk (p832).

D. Only 120 to 150 degrees: This transfers the overhead shoulder-motion range to the hip; the hip precaution starts above 90 degrees (p825; p832).
C. Only less than 90 degrees: This reverses the stated greater-than-90-degree precaution (p832).
B. No limitation on hip flexion: Avoiding excessive flexion, including with raised toilet seats, is specifically described (p832).
